newsitem.title: USA: Airports pose growing pollution problem - report.
newsitem.headline: Airports pose growing pollution problem - report.

text.p: Environmentalists called on Thursday for U.S. federal regulators to attack the growing problem of air, water and noise pollution from airports through taxes and a host of new rules.

With the huge growth in air travel, airports in many cases rival or top smokestack industries as polluters but so far have largely escaped environmental regulation, the Natural Resources Defence Council (NRDC) said in a report.

"Living near an airport is like having a refinery as a neighbour, only refineries are subject to stronger pollution controls and disclosure requirements," Jennifer Stenzel, primary author of the report, said at a briefing.
Besides noise pollution, airplane exhaust blasts out smog-forming ozone gases and chemicals used in de-icing aircraft and runways flow into waterways, the report said.

Chicago's O'Hare Airport, the nation's busiest, in 1993 spewed out almost as much smog pollution as a nearby steel plant, the report said. But airports are not held accountable for their ground level aircraft emissions, "while other major industrial sources are accordingly forced to compensate on airports' behalf as states scramble to meet mandatory emissions reductions deadlines," it said.

Citing figures from the Environmental Protection Agency, it said U.S. aircraft in 1993 emitted 350 million pounds (158 million kilos) of smog-forming gases during their and take-off, more than twice as much as in 1970.

The NRDC said airlines should be encouraged to replace ageing, inefficient aircraft by replacing the 10 percent domestic ticket tax with an aviation fuel tax. "Rather than tax passengers, we should tax the planes that are the noisiest, oldest, and most polluting," said Daniel Lashof, an NRDC scientist.

Air Transport Association spokesman David Fuscus said: "There is an intense modernisation of the airline fleet going on. We're in the middle of a $10 billion conversion of the fleet and it will have environmental benefits."

The NRDC report also said airports should be included in states' plans to meet air quality standards, should make public reports on emissions from toxic substances and should contain and treat de-icing chemicals.
